newsitem.title: CHINA: China Eastern faces tough competition -analyst.
newsitem.headline: China Eastern faces tough competition -analyst.

text.p: China's largest cellular phone maker, Eastern Communications Co, is facing tough competition and must develop its own technology and products to win, China's top brokerage firm said on Tuesday.
"With competition getting tougher, the firm's traditional sales outlets and monopoly position have been greatly weakened," Shenyin & Wanguo Securities Co said in a research paper.
"Future development will rely on its (the company's) ability for independent technical exploration, the establishment of its own famous brands and price competitiveness," it said.
Eastern Communications has both foreign currency B shares and domestic A shares listed in Shanghai.

Its products use Motorola Inc technology for all three types of cellular phone systems available in China -- analog, Global System for Mobile (GSM) Communications and code division multiple access (CDMA).
China, where four in every 1,000 people in a population of 1.2 billion have mobile phones, is the world's fourth largest portable phone market after the United States, Japan and Britain.
Analysts consider China's market potential enormous.

Eastern Communications said last Thursday in its 1996 annual report that post-tax profit for 1996 rose 14.29 percent to 291.62 million yuan ($35 million) from 255.16 in 1995 based on international accounting standards.
On domestic accounting standards, 1996 net profit edged up to 322.18 million yuan from 262.47 million yuan in 1995, the report said.
Turnover in 1996 surged 22.85 percent to 4.07 billion yuan from 3.32 billion yuan from 1995 based on international accounting standards, it said.
"The growth of post-tax profits was lower than that of turnover, indicating that profits were hit by a series of negative factors," the Shenyin & Wanguo research paper said.
About 90 percent of Eastern Communications gross profits were derived from sales of portable phones using Motorola technology, the paper said.
With competition intensifying and mobile phone prices falling in China, the firm relied too heavily on a negotiated price cut for Motorola spare parts, which had limited effect, it said.

The firm's spare parts imports from Motorola accounted for around 95 percent of 1996 costs, causing it to lose ground to foreign contenders that had directly invested and built manufacturing plants in China, it said.

"The 23 percent rise in 1996 turnover for the company was much lower than the 86 percent of 1995," the research paper said. "It was exactly the result of fierce competition from foreign counterparts."
Eastern Communications listed its B shares on August 9, 1996 and its A shares on November 26, causing a share dilution.

Earnings per share dropped to 0.77 yuan in 1996 from 1.06 yuan in 1995 on a fully diluted basis, the company's annual report said. "Facing fierce competition, the firm set up more sales and maintenance outlets around China in 1996 and managed to ensure good production and results," it said.
Analysts said Eastern Communications' excellent relations with China's Ministry of Post and Telecommunications would help it keep winning business.
Late on Monday, the firm's B shares were trading at $0.98 per share and its A shares at 23.10 yuan each.
